E071-01.notes: Redundancy: 'overseas' already means in other countries. A, C, D all redundant.

E071-02.notes: Semicolon joins two independent clauses. B comma splice; C run-on/comma splice with misplaced punctuation; D needless comma between 'an' and 'estimated'.

E071-03.notes: Sentence on war's end is off-topic for opening paragraph. A false (doesn't explain why); B false (no numbers); D false (no contradiction).

flags.note: B 'but' is just as correct as 'yet': both are coordinating conjunctions signaling contrast, and 'had never planted a seed, but newspapers... offered advice' is grammatical and logically identical. No single best answer; replace B with a non-contrast option (e.g., 'for' or 'and so').

E071-04.notes: Contrast between inexperience and available advice. C 'or' and D 'so' give wrong logic. However 'but' (B) is substitutable for 'yet' with identical meaning and punctuation.

E071-05.notes: Only D shows beginners being helped (taught by experienced gardeners). A, B, C give scheduling/attendance/organizer details.

E071-06.notes: Register: 'produced' is the formal, precise verb. A, D slangy; B 'churned up' wrong meaning.

E071-07.notes: Sentence 9 adds a further benefit -> additive 'Moreover'. B contrast wrong; C not an example; D not a result of the 40 percent statistic.

E071-08.notes: A and C have a redundant subject pronoun 'they'; D is a fragment (no finite verb).

E071-09.notes: Only A links wartime gardens to present-day community gardens. B wartime fact; C off-topic; D present but about pamphlets, not growing food.

E071-10.notes: Essay describes millions of gardens producing ~40% of fresh vegetables. A misdescribes focus; B misdescribes focus; C false (40 percent given).

E071-11.notes: Nonrestrictive appositive needs paired commas. A missing opening comma; B missing closing comma; D semicolon creates fragment.

E071-12.notes: B transitions from Fisher's proposal to the supporters who formed the association. A is irrelevant trivia (Lincoln name trap); C, D off-topic.

E071-13.notes: 'In 1913' requires simple past 'formed'. A present, B future, C present perfect clash with a specific past date.

E071-14.notes: Conciseness: A, B, D wordy/redundant ('could be like and might become', 'possibly maybe').

E071-15.notes: Only C quantifies duration (sixty-two days) to show slowness. A gives arrival month without start time; B, D irrelevant to speed.

flags.note: NO CHANGE 'its' is defensible if read as referring to 'the convoy' (subject of sentence 8): 'bridges collapsed under its [the convoy's] weight' is grammatical and logical. 'their' is still better given the nearby plural 'Trucks', but consider making the antecedent unambiguous (e.g., 'Heavy trucks sank in mud, and bridges collapsed under [their] weight').

E071-16.notes: Intended antecedent is plural 'Trucks' -> 'their'. C, D are contractions (it is/they are) and ungrammatical here.

E071-17.notes: Exposition fact is unrelated to the convoy's difficulties. A false (no reason given); B false (no crowd numbers); C false (no contradiction).

E071-18.notes: Time sequence from 1919 to presidency -> 'Decades later'. B contrast, C example, D reverses time.

E071-19.notes: Essay traces Lincoln Highway -> 1919 convoy -> Eisenhower -> Interstate system. A, B misdescribe focus; D false (Eisenhower connection given).

E071-20.notes: Only D returns to Montgolfier's small-bag observation. A, B, C don't reference the opening observation.
